painPoints.title: Do any of these sound familiar?
painPoints.intro: These are the phrases I hear most often when an SME contacts me for the first time. If any of them rings a bell, you're in good company: it's the normal state of a company that grew faster than the systems supporting it.

cards.title: "Everything lives in Excel."
cards.description: Everyone has their own spreadsheet, nobody knows the real status of projects, and information is scattered across email, Drive and WhatsApp.

cards.title: "We've already tried several tools."
cards.description: And nobody used them. The cause is well known: the tool was chosen before the process was clear, and nobody was made responsible for maintaining it.

cards.title: "We're growing, but our organisation isn't keeping up."
cards.description: More clients and more orders bring more mistakes, more rework — and whole days spent putting out fires.

cards.title: "We received an ERP proposal, but..."
cards.description: Five-figure numbers, 12-month timelines and a sales pitch that's hard to evaluate. Before signing, it pays to have someone on your side of the table reading the proposal.

painPoints.closing: Recognised yourself in two or more? A 15-minute call is enough to measure the size of the problem — and see the first step towards solving it.

whatIsVA.title: What I do, in practice

points.title: Diagnosis before any proposal
points.description: I spend one to two weeks understanding how the company actually works — not how it's written down that it works. You get a simple map: what exists, what's missing, and what it costs per month to keep going as is.

points.title: Translating proposals and vendors
points.description: When you receive a software proposal, I read it with you, translate the tech-speak and ask the vendor the hard questions — so you buy what you need, not what they want to sell you.

points.title: Custom systems, built on what you already use
points.description: I connect the tools you already have (invoicing software, Google Workspace, Drive) and build in low-code — tools that let you create systems without programming from scratch — a dashboard where you see the status of every project and who's doing what.

points.title: Implementation in phases, with visible results
points.description: No 18-month projects. Small, measurable improvements, with the first delivery visible within a few weeks — often paying for itself through the cleanup of subscriptions and tools the company pays for without using.

points.title: Ongoing maintenance and protection
points.description: A system without an owner goes back to Excel within three months. I stay after delivery: team questions, real backups, access under control, and a written plan for when something fails.

whatIsVA.highlight: I am, in practice, the IT department your company doesn't have — and doesn't want to have — in-house. With 20 years of software engineering behind me, and no interest in selling anyone's software.

services.title: How can I help your company?
services.description: Diagnosis, technical intermediation with vendors and custom digital operating systems — in phases, with visible results.

whyChooseVA.title: Why an External Technical Director?
whyChooseVA.description: SMEs that have grown past the startup stage live in an uncomfortable gap: too structured to justify an ERP and an IT team, too grown to keep living in Excel. That's the space I occupy — on your side of the table, with no commissions from any vendor.

benefits.title: Total vendor independence
benefits.description: I recommend what serves the business, including "don't buy anything" or "make better use of what you already pay for" — like the purchasing module of an invoicing tool a client had been paying for, unused, for months.

benefits.title: 20 years of software engineering
benefits.description: Consulting and software development experience at the service of your technology decisions — no sales pressure, and the hard questions asked by someone who speaks the vendors' language.

benefits.title: Results in phases, within weeks
benefits.description: Never "big bang" 18-month projects. Each phase delivers a visible, measurable result before moving on to the next.

benefits.title: Documentation and autonomy
benefits.description: Everything documented, accounts and access always in the company's name, tools with large communities. If one day you want to work with someone else, they pick up where I left off.

aboutMe.title: The IT person your company doesn't have — and doesn't want to hire
aboutMe.bio:
I'm a software engineer with 20 years of experience in consulting and software development. Today I work with Portuguese SMEs that have grown to the point where operations live in scattered Excel files and tools that don't talk to each other.

I do two things: I act as the technical intermediary when the company needs to evaluate vendors and systems (I translate proposals, ask the hard questions, prevent bad purchases), and I directly build custom systems — automations, integrations and management dashboards in low-code — adapted to the way the team already works.

items.title: Simplicity
items.description: I always choose the simplest tool that solves the problem. Many SMEs would run perfectly on a simple CRM and a central information hub — and end up with sophisticated platforms nobody uses.

items.title: Independence
items.description: No commissions from any vendor. I recommend what serves the business, even when the recommendation doesn't benefit me — including saying "this part isn't for me".

items.title: Compatibility
items.description: I connect what you already use — Outlook, Teams, Google Drive or Gmail — so your tools start talking to each other, and I automate what's repetitive. I never push you towards an ERP or a new, complex system when the right answer is simpler.

items.title: Measurable results
items.description: Every phase has a number attached: hours saved per week, subscriptions eliminated, response time reduced. What gets measured gets improved.

hero.title: Technology with method, not on impulse
hero.subtitle: Most companies start with the tool: buy the software and figure it out later — which is why most systems end up abandoned. I work in the opposite order: first understand how the business actually works, then decide what deserves attention, and only then implement — in small phases, with visible results from the first weeks.

differentiators.title: What sets me apart
differentiators.description: An External Technical Director occupies a place that consultants, agencies and freelancers leave empty — the place of the person who answers for the result and sits on the client's side of the table.

items.title: From traditional consultants
items.description: The consultant listens, advises and delivers a report. I design and build: the diagnosis ends in working systems, not PowerPoints — and I stay afterwards, for maintenance, team questions and evolution.

items.title: From agencies and ERP implementers
items.description: Agencies live off selling big projects; I live off long relationships with small systems that work. And when an agency really is the right answer, I sit on your side of the table: I translate the proposal, tighten the requirements and oversee the delivery.

items.title: From automation freelancers
items.description: The freelancer executes one piece well and disappears. I think through the whole system before the piece — the anchor question is "how many clients do you have today, and how many do you want?" — and I take on ongoing responsibility: maintenance, security, backups.

cta.title: The first step takes 15 minutes
cta.description: A no-obligation call to understand how your operation works today and whether it makes sense to move on to a diagnosis.

items.question: What do you actually do, day to day?
items.answer: I act as the external IT department the company doesn't have. That doesn't always mean building systems from scratch, the initial diagnosis can end in three different ways: making better use of what you already pay for and aren't using, connecting tools you already have so they start talking to each other, or building a custom piece when there's no simpler alternative that solves it. From there, I'm also available for practical configurations, the team's day-to-day questions, and evaluating or negotiating software vendor proposals on your behalf.

items.question: Can you deal directly with my software vendors?
items.answer: Yes, it's one of the most requested roles. If you've received a proposal and aren't sure it makes sense, or you're midway through an implementation and need someone on your side tracking it technically, I can read contracts and proposals, and speak directly with the vendor, to make sure you buy what you need — not what they want to sell you.

items.question: Won't this turn into a huge, expensive ERP-style project, even if the initial idea is small?
items.answer: It's the right fear to have, and the answer lies in the method: I work in small phases, with results visible within weeks, and whatever gets built always sits on top of the tools you already use, never against them. A real example: an 8-person SME asked me to evaluate an ERP proposal of €32,000 and 14 months of implementation. What they actually needed: project tracking and purchasing control — was solved with a module of their invoicing software they were already paying for without using, plus a project dashboard built in 6 weeks. Final cost: a fraction of the proposal.

items.question: If we decide to build something custom, do I become hostage to whoever built it?
items.answer: It's not the rule, but if that's the path: I use established low-code tools, not closed proprietary code; everything gets documented; and accounts and data always stay in your name, never mine.

items.question: We've already tried several tools and nobody used them. Why would it be different now?
items.answer: It's the most common outcome, and it has a well-known cause: the tool was chosen before the process was clear, and nobody was made responsible for maintaining it afterwards. I work in reverse: first we map how the team actually works, only then do we choose or build something, and ongoing support is part of the work from day one.

items.question: What if I become dependent on a single person?
items.answer: A fair objection. That's why documentation of processes and systems is a mandatory deliverable, not optional, and access always stays in your name. If one day you want to work with someone else, they pick up where I left off.

items.question: I don't have time for IT projects right now.
items.answer: It's precisely because you don't have time that the format is this one: I take it on, you validate. The diagnosis takes up only a few hours of your time in total; from there, your side of the effort is approving decisions, not managing work.
